utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The accused may be seated. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. For the Prosecution, Mr. Daryl Mundis and I, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, co-counsel Stephane Bourgon, and Mirna Milanovic, assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, with Rodney Dixon and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to bid good morning to the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and the interpreters in the booth. Today we're going to continue with the examination of the witness who started to testify yesterday. This examination is envisaged for another 15 minutes, upon which we will proceed with the cross-examination, after which we will have a new witness that will be called. So have the witness brought in, please. Mr. Cvijanovic, you may be seated. I shall give the floor to the Prosecution who will continue the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when we stopped yesterday, you had told us that at some point on 26 January 1993 you were taken to a school. Do you recall testifying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear it now. Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when we stopped yesterday, you had told us that at some point on 26 January 1993 you were taken to a school. Do you recall testifying to that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the hill, we came to the coffee bar, the billiard room. We waited for everyone to gather, and then we headed towards the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us the name of the school or the location of the school.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school is in Lasva. It used to be called Ivo Lola Ribar Elementary School Lasva. That was its name at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you arrive at that school?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly about 3.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what happened at the elementary school in Lasva after your arrival.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left the coffee bar, there were two soldiers of the BH army. And as we moved, fire was opened. Then we turned back. And then one of them came out, and he had a code in Arabic, and then they stopped shooting. So we headed together with them towards the school. They were offering guarantees to us, as they saw that we were frightened. They said that everything would be all right, in spite of what had happened. They were armed. We all had rifles as well, and we headed straight towards the school. When we reached Velimir Kristo's house - this is very near the school - the police of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were there. I recognised some of my neighbours. Two of them were wearing police uniforms. One was called Rusmir Sisic and the other Halac Nedzad. As we walked, we had to leave our weapons in a pile, whatever we had, as we went towards the school. We were spat upon, abused, cursed, and so on. Once we reached the school, we found some civilians there, our family members, our relatives, fathers, wives, children, parents, et cetera. We were separated so that the women and the children were put in one classroom and we men were taken to another classroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what happened in the room where the men were taken.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we arrived, there were some guys there that we didn't know. The only people we knew was Hazim Barucija. He was wearing a military uniform. He was our teacher. He used to be a teacher in the elementary school. He was a reserve officer. I think he had the rank of captain first class. He met us there together with the soldiers whom we did not know, because they weren't from our part of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, witness, when anyone else from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina entered the classroom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, while we were there, some soldiers were coming in from their positions. They would enter the classroom. They took off pieces of our clothing and uniforms, whatever they liked, jacket, trousers, shirts. They mistreated us, beat us, and then they'd just leave. We didn't dare say anything. We were forced to look down with our heads bent towards the desks, and this went on until Mr. Serif Patkovic arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened after Serif Patkovic arrived at the Lasva Elementary School.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this mistreatment went on. At one point in time they would let us go to the toilet or see our family members. I went out to see whether my family was there. When I came back -- when I went there, I saw our women and children and the elderly, who were out of their minds, who were crying. My wife -- no, I'm sorry, Zvonko Rajic's wife and her two daughters came up to me. The little girls were crying, and they hugged me and they asked me, "Where is our daddy?" That is, the younger daughter, Anita, asked me where her daddy was. I couldn't tell her what happened. So then I decided when she asked whether her father was alive, and as I kept quiet, she noticed that something was wrong -- before that, they had already been told that he had been killed, and I said also that he had been killed and that he had been left behind on the ground. My mother was there and my father and my brother was with me. I could have stayed there for two or three minutes because the soldier came to fetch us immediately to take us back to the classroom where the men were. Only a couple of us left that classroom, those who had the courage to do so. Then a soldier came in, and he ordered all of us to get up and then a gentleman walked through the door. That was the first time in my life for me to see him close up. He was wearing a black vest. He had a small beard. He was wearing a police uniform, and he was carrying his bag probably and the bag of the late Zvonko, containing documents that Zvonko had about us, with our particulars, his diaries and all those things. He said hello in Arabic, or some words in Arabic, and then he said, "I am Mr. Serif Patkovic." He had come to meet us. "And as I call out your name, will he get up and say yes." Then the gentleman ordered us to sit down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how long did you remain at the Lasva elementary school that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was about 3.30. And then in the evening, about 10.30, they took us out of the school. Some were boarded on buses; others went on foot, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to you as you left the Lasva elementary school about 10.30 that day.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman came again and said, as he called out a name the person should come out the door. And we were waiting. And as he called people out, they went out the door. When we came out of the school, they have a staircase. There is the school playground. And the school stadium was full of troops, and where there was a football pitch, which was full of troops. And in front of the school was the basketball playground, and again it was full of troops. The soldiers were lined up in two rows, to our left and our right. And as we were coming out, we had to pass through these lines, and they beat us as -- if you fell down you're done for. They would hit you with their rifles. They would kick you with their hands, whatever he could get hold of. And this line was from the school up until the local community building, which was about 50 to 100 metres away, I don't know exactly. There were a couple of cars there, and with our heads bent, and our arms behind our heads, with our heads bowed, they were beating us, and then some people were boarded onto the vehicles and others took a shortcut, which was also lined with troops, leading towards the railway station. And they were too beaten as they went towards the station. As for me, one of the soldiers pushed me into some sort of a vehicle, and they beat us and they went along the road. When we reached the station, Lasva station - it is the railway and bus station - buses were lined up there, and, again, there were lots of soldiers, police, many vehicles, et cetera. For a moment the vehicles were stopped there. I was taken off the vehicle. Then I was beaten up again. And from the blows I couldn't stand any more. I was lying in the snow. And as a soldier went by, he would kick me or hit me with his rifle. And as I was lying there, in the meantime, those who were going on foot from the school towards the station, as they arrived they were beaten and shoved into buses. I was lying bloodied and beaten up down there, and then a group of soldiers came. They lifted me up and lent me against the bus. Then they started beating me again. Two of them were holding me under the armpits and leaning me against the bus, as I could no longer stand on my own two feet, because I was all beaten up. I couldn't really see. I could only see a little on one eye. My jaws were broken in two places. I had a head fracture, a nose fracture. I could just see a little with my left eye. And the gentleman spoke to me and said if I fell down once again, I would be beaten twice as hard. Of course, as soon as they let go, I would drop to the ground again and they continued mistreating me. They put a knife to my neck, asking where the Herzegovina people were, where our artillery was, all kinds of fabrications. And none of it was true. These were just lies. These people were convinced that we had all those things. I didn't know those men. They were not locals. They were not from our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then suddenly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt, but due to time constraints I feel I must. Were you then taken to a different location? And if so, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They continued beating me. And then a gentleman arrived with the police and they started arguing between them. In the meantime, they let me fall again on the snow-covered concrete. And while they argued amongst themselves, one gentleman, I heard him, said, "This is the first and last time that you go with us on an operation and for you to share our booty with us." And while they were quarreling, some soldiers picked me up and shoved me again into a vehicle. And then I started losing consciousness. They drove me for a while. I felt sick. They cursed me. They said that they would roast me, that they would throw me to the fishes, that all the others would be killed, during this short drive. And then I felt the brakes and the vehicle was stopped, the one I was in. The argument started up again. I could no longer see anything. I could only hear, because my eyes were closed. And the argument was between the same troops that were up there - I think they were the police of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and the forces of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- where were you taken or where was the next time you became aware of where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were quarreling, they took me out of the vehicle, and I realised that I was at a crossroads where there was a checkpoint held by the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the crossroads for Sarajevo, Kakanj, Zenica and Busovaca. I fainted then, and I don't remember anything after that. I woke up in prison of the KP Dom in Zenica, the prison in Zenica, and I was lying on a prison cot without a mattress or anything. I think this was maybe two days later or a day or two later; I don't know. That is where I woke up. That is what I am conscious of. I was woken up by pain. I was vomiting blood. I was coughing. And that's what brought me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did anyone else tell you where you were during the period that you were unconscious?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that later. I'm not conscious of it. I was -- this was passed on to me. Mr. Bakir Alispahic told me this, when after spending some time in prison, when I was taken for interrogation to make statements and to write statements - we kept doing this throughout the time we were in prison, not just me but all of us - and then Mr. Bakir Alispahic told me that he had taken me from those forces, that he had given me cigarettes, none of which I could remember. But when I came to, the cigarettes were in my pocket, blue Ronhill cigarettes, and the lighter of the police of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I've kept it to this day. I think I have it at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive any form of medical treatment for the injuries you received?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was regaining consciousness, I heard conversations on the basis of which I concluded that these were my neighbours and relatives who were there with me. I was in a corner on this cot, and as I turned around, I fell to the ground. They were in another corner. This is an enormous prison room with benches and a couple of these cots. We spent all day there. They were not allowed to come up to me. They didn't know who I was, because I wasn't wearing my uniform. Everything had been taken off me. I only had a T-shirt and my underwear. Around my neck I had a chain and on it was my wedding ring. As I fell, I turned around. As I was covered in blood, I couldn't see anything. I couldn't talk. I had two fractures on my jaw, I was vomiting blood, I was urinating blood. There was blood coming through my ears from the blows. And then Dragan Kristo and Velimir Kristo came up to me in the prison. They were standing there wondering whether it was me or not. I could hear them talking, "Is it Zeljko or not?" And then Ivica Filipovic got up and said, "Don't go up to him. You don't know who he is. We can only have problems on that score." My brother was there too, and he didn't recognise me either. And when Velo and Dragan had come up to me, as I had fallen, my chain and wedding ring fell off. They knew me. We were friends, and my brother -- everyone knew I was wearing that. And then they recognised me. Velo swore and said, "My God, it's Zeljko" . Just then the police walked in, the guards who were guarding us, and they started yelling at them. They stopped. Of course, they were terrified. And then this gentleman asked, "Who gave you permission to go up to him?" They said that I was a Chetnik, that -- all kinds of things, that I should be killed, and then they said, "But it's our relative. He's one of us. He fell down." And then a gentleman who was then in command walked in. I think he was from Tetovo. His surname started with an "A." He was an elderly man. I think he was some sort of a chief in the prison then. And I can say in all frankness that he was very fair towards all of us when he was on duty but when he left, all kinds of things happened. He worked during working hours. Then he would go home, after which all kinds of things would happen. And then he said to Dragan and Velo Kristo, that they were responsible for me. After that, maybe half an hour later, two soldiers came and took me to the premises where the office was of this -- people -- man who was in charge. Mr. Bakir Alispahic was there. I couldn't see too well, and I was very ill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness -- thank you, witness. I'm afraid we're out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] I now give the floor to counsel for the Defence for the cross-examination. Let me add that it's now 9.30. We will have a -- the break, as usual, as 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cvijanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. Before I start my cross-examination, I should like, with the Court's indulgence, to caution you and to say that the two of us speak the same language, so we could go ahead quickly and ask questions and give answers very rapidly. However, we have the interpreters to consider, because our cross-examination has to be interpreted for people in the courtroom and for the benefit of the public. So I should like to ask you to make pauses between my question and your answer and listen through your headset to hears whether the interpretation has been finished. That will facilitate understanding for one and all in the courtroom. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to start off by asking you some general questions. Yesterday you spoke about the geographical position of Lasva and the surrounding villages and hamlets; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Dusina, Lasva, Donja Visnjica, Brdo, and the hamlets of Rajici are all villages and hamlets which belong to the local commune of Lasva; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The local commune of Lasva belonged to the Zenica municipality, and it was the last local commune as you go towards the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and towards Kakanj too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many of the inhabitants of the Lasva local commune - that is to say, all the villages taken together - went to secondary schools and other schools in Zenica and many inhabitants actually worked in Zenica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Zenica was a rather large town and industrial centre and people found a livelihood there, so it was normal for them to go to work there because it was a nearby big town. Yes; that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Lasva itself and the hamlet of Rajici next to Lasva were in a valley bordering the River Bosna; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's where my family house was, my family, and I lived there ever since I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other village, Donja Visnjica, Brdo, the hamlet of Kegelj, they were all high up on the hills, the slopes of the hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donja Visnjica became a part of the village of Rajici and it was a whole; whereas Dusina and Brdo were separate ask they were several kilometres away from Donja Visnjica and the village of Rajici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could get to those villages by climbing up the mountain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that from the village of Dusina to Lasva the distance was about 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's roughly it, if you take a round-about road, the road that existed then and still exists today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Lasva and the hamlet of Rajici, which is where your house is, up to the hamlet of Brdo, that's about 1 and a half kilometres; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take the round-about road, if -- if you take the road, yes, but if you take a shortcut, then it's closer, and it would be approximately a kilometre. So that is going from my -- through my village, there's Donja Visnjica, there's a stream that cuts across this area and separates us. That was the Croatian inhabitants with just a few Muslim houses there. Now, behind those homesteads was a large rock and there was a relay station up there on the cliff and this was right underneath. It was called Donja Visnjica, and that's what we called Brdo up there, Vranjaca Brdo. That was the elevation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to get an overall picture of the local commune of Lasva itself and to project this image to all the participants in the courtroom and for me to be able to continue with my questioning, I'm going to show you a videotape taken from a helicopter. So I should like to ask you to tell us whether we can recognise the place. May we have the tape played, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, can you recognise the footage that we're showing now?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Lasva. And before that, we saw Dusina, not Lasva. This is Lasva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the local commune, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we saw the village of Dusina, Brdo, and finally Lasva, towards the end, with the Lasva flowing into the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the fact that the witness has recognised and identified the area, I should like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be DH1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the tape, we saw the general configuration of the land, the lie of the land, in which the villages and hamlets were located of the Lasva local commune; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I am sure you'll agree with me when I say that from Brdo or from the hill, you can't see the Kegelj hamlet because between them there's another small hill.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't agree with that, because you can see some houses, two Serb houses, in fact, belonging to the Kalajdzics, Simo Kalajdzic and Djordje Kalajdzic. So those are the first two houses. And behind them you can see Kegelj Jure's house. There were three Kegelj brothers, in fact, Jozo, Jure, and Stipo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's move on to another area that you testified about yesterday. You stated that from 1992 you were a member of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you belonged to an HVO unit which was located in Lasva; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your unit did not belong to the HVO brigade called Jure Francetic, which had it headquarters in Zenica, although Lasva was in the Zenica municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not belong to that. It belonged to another brigade from Busovaca, and it was called Nikola Subic Zrinski, that's the brigade it belonged to. And all the support to the people during those events was lent by people from Busovaca, not those from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that your unit at no point in time from 1992 until the end of the conflict with the HVO was never subordinated to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it was the Croatian Defence Council and was a platoon which was attached to Busovaca, so it was a regular army, one or the other. And we, as military-able men, were able -- each citizen was able to choose which army he would join, whether the BH army or the HVO army, because they were the two legal army that is existed there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you will agree that the HVO had its own chain of command. Your command was in Busovaca and the Main Staff was in Grude; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my immediate superior was Zvonko Rajic, and the main command was at Busovaca. Now, who was in command there, I really can't say. I am an ordinary soldier, rank and file, and I can't know the answer to that question. So for me that's something that I don't know. All I can say is this, and I stand by it: That we were there and that we received orders from Busovaca. And I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that there was a deterioration in relations with the BH army at the beginning of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of 1992, I would say, there was some lack of understanding and tensions raised. 1993 was the culmination of all this, when a war conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure you know that on the 15th of January, by the top leadership of the HVO, an order was issued for combat readiness for the HVO units and that this should be raised to the top level combat readiness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that. Or in fact of that. Perhaps. Perhaps my superior who was there knew about that, but as I say, as an ordinary soldier I couldn't have known about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know that it was ordered that all Muslims in units that did not respect HVO orders should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam, that's wrong. That's a mistake. It was the other way round. All the Croats and the Serbs who were in that area received orders to be disarmed and -- quite simply, that they should be disarmed. And they did not recognise it as a legal army. And this can be borne out and confirmed by my brother, who was Miroslav Rajic. I hope you have him in your books. And from the very first day - he's a cousin living in Rajic too - and from the very first day, he joined up with the BH army, when we joined up with the HVO. And ultimately he was disarmed. And even if he was a BH army member and was not involved in anything when these things were taking place, but he was taken off to prison just like the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that detailed explanation. However, I should like to ask you, Mr. Cvijanovic, in future to answer my questions with a yes-or-no answer. That will be sufficient, of course, if that is possible. But I'm sure you are aware of this, that an order was issued to all forces in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to shut off all directions and access from Zenica and place them under the control of the operative zone. Is that something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order also included an order that all Muslim transports with equipment and weapons should be seized and placed at the disposal of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that either, whether an order of that kind existed. As I said before, I'm just an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, in order to remind you of this order, to have the order by the Main Staff of the HVO, dated the 15th of January, 1993, shown to you. And we have supplied sufficient copies of that order for all parties in the court, pursuant to the Court's instructions. Unfortunately, it hasn't been interpreted or translated into any of the working languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Prosecution like to say something at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object on the grounds that the witness has repeatedly said he knows nothing of this and there's not a proper foundation for the witness to be shown this document at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this objection, the witness taking note of the document, can he tell us whether he has seen it before or had knowledge of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Defence give us -- tell us more about the document and where it comes from, in view of the fact that the witness has never seen or heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document contains an order by the Main Staff, the headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council. It is dated the 15th of January, 1993 and demands full combat readiness of all HVO units, especially with respect to the forces of the BH army or, rather, the Muslim forces and gives an overall picture of the causes of the conflicts that ensued in the Lasva area. In view of the fact that we would like -- we cannot through this witness ascertain the authenticity of this document, I propose, Your Honours, that for the moment we just identify the document as being a Defence document so that later on, as a relevant document, relevant to the Defence, we could use it. Could the document please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point the Prosecution would have to reserve its position. This is the first time we have seen this document, and it is not in one of the official working languages of the Tribunal. So at this point the Prosecution is unable to take any position with respect to this document, so we would respectfully reserve our rights with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall then mark the document for identification and we will see how -- what status to give it ultimately. I should like to ask the Defence in future that when it produces a document to have it translated, if that is possible, at least in English, to allow the Prosecution to look through it. Having said that - and can we have it marked for identification from the registrar now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document will be DH2 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have understood your instructions; however, we have this problem of translation for documents for the cross-examination, which we discussed, and I don't think this is the opportune moment for me to go into that. We shall do our best to ensure that the documents are translated for the cross-examination, but, quite simply, all the documents have been returned to us from the Dusina case by the registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, I should now like to ask you to continue our conversation. You said that at the beginning of 1993 open conflicts broke out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 15th of January, the situation in Busovaca deteriorated dramatically and an armed conflict took place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this: Is it true and correct that after the 15th of January the situation in the municipality of Busovaca changed and open conflicts broke out between the HVO and the Bosnian army -- Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not after the 15th of January. There was increased tension, and that was quite obvious. The Muslim population began to group itself and separate itself; so did the Croatian population. There was tension, but there weren't any operations until the 23rd or 24th of January of that same year, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The population of Lasva knew full well about the conflicts in Busovaca because a large number of refugees from that area passed through the villages and hamlets of Lasva, of the Lasva river valley; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was no conflict up until then. Yes, there were certain small -- minor incidents, and those incidents for the most part occurred because there was tension, there was provocation, minor details of that kind. There was some shooting, and that instilled fear on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that this tension spread to Lasva and the villages in Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tensions in the Lasva river valley, its villages and hamlets, began far before that. It was in the summer of 1992, when the Serb population was expulsed and mistreated, expelled from the area, because they came to ask protection from the Croatian Defence Council and we gave them that protection, so that tensions grew straight away as a result of that. So that started long before the Busovaca affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that it was in Busovaca that the conflicts broke out. Is it true that what you meant at the time was the open armed conflict on the night between the 20th and 21st -- in the night between the 20th and 21st of January, 1993 and you could hear it all going on? Explosions could be heard very well both in Dusina and other hamlets of the Lasva river valley?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question slowly and what response you expect from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this: Did you state yesterday that in Busovaca there was an open conflict that took place -- and now I'm suggesting the following to you -- that that conflict and the fighting that went on could be heard loud and clear because of the explosions that took place there, both in Dusina and in other areas of Lasva?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that explosions were heard, but not at Dusina. There was no shooting at Dusina, madam. Dusina is Lasva. Yes, there was shooting in Busovaca, where you could hear explosions. And all of us - of course, the locals - a local who was there and who was neutral - we were in our houses and everything was quiet - but large numbers of BH army members, soldiers, were coming in because they were taking up their positions along Kula, Sudine, Lugovi, and so on, Merdani. They were passing that way through Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the refugees coming from Busovaca and the surrounding villages, you learnt that several hundred Bosniaks were taken to the Kaonik camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. While we were in Lasva ourselves, not a single refugee came to Lasva nor did we know anything about it, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, your unit held a point -- checkpoint in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not hold a checkpoint in Lasva. It manned a checkpoint in the canyon with Busovaca forces. It is at the triangle area there. If you know the restaurant of Olympik, which exists today, and that was where the checkpoint was -- and the soldiers who were in Lasva for the population would take shifts on a daily basis, and that was your work duty. It was like a work obligation and work duty. That's how it was. You took shifts. Two soldiers at a time. There was -- there were two shifts, the first shift and the second shift; the day shift and the night shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. For us to be able to follow this next portion of questions that I'm going to ask you, I should like the Trial Chamber and the witness and everybody else to be shown a map of the Lasva river valley. Could the map be placed -- be distributed and placed on the overhead projector, please. I apologise. The technical booth has not received a copy to have map, so could we place the map on the overhead projector. We haven't got a tape of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, using this map, could you indicate to us with the pointer you have in front of you each place mentioned: Lasva, Donja Visnjica, Brdo, and Dusina.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is it, from the Bosna and Lasva confluence we have the BH army post here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us on the map.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the BH army point. This black arrow is a bridge, I think. And from this bridge, around this curve, was another checkpoint of the Croatian Defence Council. This was no man's land. It was the space in between. And you would go to the free zone over here. This is Lasva. That was a station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but next to the station there was the cafe owned by Faruk Barucija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, next to the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's where the HVO checkpoint was.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not where the HVO checkpoint was. The shop received -- obtained the premises of this shop to use for their own purposes, and there were problems quite often there because there was a flag set up which was taken down very often and incidents broke out in that shop. But the HVO never had its checkpoint in the shop itself there, at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the HVO did control the passage through that area.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. Everybody could move around quite freely. There was no control there at all. As far as control is concerned, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army set up a checkpoint on the bridge crossing the Lasva river, at the crossroads here. That's where there was a wooden bridge. There's a concrete bridge there now. They even placed tank mines there. And that was held -- that checkpoint was held by our neighbour, people who grew up with me. We grew up together. I could give you many of their names. I would meet them and I very often had problems when I was going back home after doing my duty. They wouldn't allow me free passage, they asked to see my identification papers. Quite simply, there was provocation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Lasva, we come to the hamlet of Rajici, which is also inhabited by Croats and where all adults were members of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a purely Croatian village. It's here. This is the stream, and this is where the village of Rajici was. It was part of Donja Visnjica. Exactly where I was showing now, this was part of Donja Visnjica. It belonged to Donja Visnjica, according to municipality maps, as only the Rajici lived there; that is, the family name. They were all relatives and they called this hamlet Rajici and that is how it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, let me ask you, in view of the HVO checkpoint that you just pointed to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. The Prosecutor has an objection to make. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not so much an objection. I'm unsure as to whether my colleague is going to somehow describe for the record what the witness is pointing to or perhaps have him mark the map, but he has been pointing to and discussing a number of points for the past few minutes, none of which will be reflected in the written record of trial, absent an explanation or markings being made to the map. And I simply point that out before we get much further down -- down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness needs to confirm, in answer to your question, that the localities mentioned on the map do indeed correspond to the localities he's familiar with. So he should confirm that the village of Rajici is indeed there, that his village of Lasva is as marked on the map, and that the control put up by the HVO was indeed at the point where the two rivers meet, that is, next to the wooden bridge. So he should answer your questions with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, you have understood the observations by the President, so will you please confirm that you recognise the map of the Lasva area.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask this map to be marked for identification as a map recognised by the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you also confirm that on this map you did identify the locality of Lasva, the position of the railway station on it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The spot where the village of Rajici is, that you come from.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That close to the confluence of the Lasva River and the Bosna River you marked a checkpoint held by the HVO and the other one, manned by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the confluence and not at the railway station, as you said. Next to Faruk Barucija's coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map also shows the localities and the elevations of the hamlets of Brdo, Crna and Dusina. Since the witness has recognised this map as a whole, including the altitudes, I would like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation Continues] ... DH3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, now that we have recalled all the localities that are relevant for this case, would you agree with me if I say that if the road towards Busovaca is blocked the only way to come from Zenica to Kacuni, Busovaca, or other places in the direction of Sarajevo leads through Lasva and Dusina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. The road was never blocked. There was just a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question. If the road to Busovaca is blocked, is it only way to reach the area of Kacuni, Sarajevo, et cetera, via Lasva and Dusina, since the road from Visoko had already been occupied by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. But the road was not blocked. The road was open to traffic, and everyone could use it. But just as at the BH army checkpoint did controls and checks because of smuggling and all kinds of things, but road was open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This road through Lasva and Dusina leads through a mountainous area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to remind you of a meeting which you also mentioned and which happened at the local commune of Lasva a day or two prior to the conflict of the 26th of January. Namely, is it true that at the local commune premises of Lasva a meeting was held between representatives of the army a day or two prior to the conflict and you attended that meeting, as well as Zvonko Rajic, Ivica Filipovic, Anto Kristo, Rados Dragan, as representatives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right. A meeting was held, but I was working at the checkpoint at the time, and it is not true that I attended, but I do know that a meeting was held. And there were representatives from Kotor Varos and Vrhovina, refugees who had been expelled and they attended the meeting. I'm aware of that meeting but I didn't attend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had indicated that there was a great danger of a unit from Busovaca where there was an open armed conflict going on with the army being present in the area of Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting, so I can't assert that. But I can pass on what I heard at the time, and that is that Mr. Zvonko Rajic and a representative from Kotor Varos --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, if you don't know exactly what happened, I won't ask you about it, because it is best to speak about things you know from personal knowledge in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't attend. I can only tell you what I was told. And I wasn't there and I can pass on what I was told as to what happened at the meeting and what the decision that was taken was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Zvonko Rajic rejected all proposals of the army and that he made a statement for television to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I told you I wasn't there. I personally, and my colleagues at the checkpoint afterwards, were told what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now discuss the events of the 25th and the 26th of January. On the 25th of January, in the afternoon, you were in Dusina in the hamlet of Kegelj in Marko Rajic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't in Dusina at all. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that on that day two members of the army from Dusina were arrested. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam. They were not from Dusina but from Brdo, Mehmedalija. And we were not in Dusina but we were in a patrol going from Crna towards Busovaca and not at Dusina at Marko Rajic's house. That is erroneous information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do know that two members of the army were captured and arrested on that day.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, you had on you a Winchester Austrian sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true. I had a Kalashnikov rifle, which has a number. And in that patrol these two gentlemen who were arrested, they were provoking us and they were even threatening us that we couldn't pass through the village. Zvonko Rajic was there and a group of people, a group of eight men, and these two guys were disarmed because they threatened, they wouldn't let us pass through the village of Kegelj, not at Dusina. And then Zvonko ordered that they be disarmed and they went to the local commune, reported them, and then they returned their weapons without any mistreatment or any problems. This can be confirmed by others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were patrolling, together with Zvonko Rajic and another eight members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise; may I add something? In that patrol, there should have been members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with us together, but they refused because they didn't want to do it together with us. For them we were the aggressors; that is how they considered us at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that your families had been moved to the Kegelj hamlet. Is it true that the families from Lasva, Brdo, and other hamlets nearby were moved on the 25th of January to the Kegelj settlement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them. My family and some other families, out of fear of their own free will, they grouped together. It is true that some families with their children had sought shelter in the house of Marko Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, they moved there because you were preparing for the conflict the next day.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not because of our preparations. Because if a man was preparing himself, he wouldn't be in bed asleep; he would be on his position. You know how a man who is preparing for a conflict acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, let us go back to the second part of your testimony yesterday and today. Yesterday and today you were saying under oath, before this Trial Chamber, truthfully.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I truthfully recounted everything I had experienced and what I can still recollect. I may have omitted to mention something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before yesterday's testimony, you made a statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke about all those events truthfully, to the best of your recollection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to look at the statement that you gave to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal so that we might check the truthfulness of what you just said. We have prepared a sufficient number of copies in English and Bosnian of Mr. Cvijanovic's statement. And could you be given a copy of the statement in B/C/S because that is the statement the two of us understand best; isn't that right? Is that the statement you gave? Can you confirm that the first page contains your particulars correctly and on the last page is the certification that the statement was read out to you and that you understood it and that the same may be used before the International Criminal Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, that we have identified the statement, I would like to ask you to answer my questions as precisely as you can. Yesterday, answering a question from the Prosecution, you said that a relative of yours on the 26th of January in the morning, a little before 6.00, came from Zvonko Rajic and told you that you had been attacked and that you all needed to go to the billiard room where you used to meet anyway. And this is noted on page 62, line 2 of the unauthorised transcript of yesterday's proceedings. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you received an order from Zvonko Rajic to gather there, to meet there, which is noted on page 62, line 24 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what this relative told me that Zvonko had ordered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement of the 11th of November, 1999, which you have in front of you, on page 2, third paragraph, in the B/C/S version, you stated "I woke up and went out. There was shooting towards my house. I grabbed my rifle and went to the coffee bar where the HVO gathered." Is that what it says in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these two statements, Mr. Cvijanovic, different?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite normal that they should be different. I don't know how this was translated and written down. I didn't have a watch. I told you roughly what time it was. But it is correct that this relative came, that I grabbed my rifle, and I went where I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not right that you got up and ran to the billiard room straight away, where the HVO meeting place was.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you said. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, on page 2 of the statement that you provided for the Prosecution earlier, the fourth sentence reads: "I grabbed my rifle and I went to a coffee bar where the HVO had their meeting place." You did not mention your relative. So the two statements are not identical.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says here, that is true. I don't know how the gentleman wrote that down, but I stand by what I said, that all this happened the way it did and it can be verified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in court you stated that "Zvonko Rajic tried to contact Busovaca but he couldn't because it was difficult to establish a connection." This was noted on page 63, lines 13, 14 of the LiveNote. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your earlier statement, which you have in front of you, you stated that "Zvonko Rajic was in contact with the command in Busovaca." This can be found in the middle of the third paragraph. And you stated: "He was in contact with the HVO command if Busovaca." Do you agree with me that again these two statements differ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday I didn't deny that Zvonko was in contact, that it was with difficulty that he reached them but on a couple of occasions he did contact them. So I don't see any discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But clearly the transcript does not reflect that because it cannot be found in the transcript. You have now cleared that up. I will continue with my questions. Yesterday, in answer to a question from the Prosecution as to whether two BH soldiers that you spoke to in the coffee bar said how many soldiers there were on their side, how many there were roughly, you said that they didn't mention how many soldiers they had but that they did mention units and their names. And this appears on page 66, lines 14 to 22 of the transcript. Did you say that yesterday, Mr. Cvijanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that they didn't mention a figure but they were astonished and they said, "Why would we need so many soldiers?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecution in 1999, at the end of the fourth paragraph, last sentence, you said, "They were surprised and said that there was no need for them to bring 1.500 soldiers to the area." You didn't mention the units. Is it true that again there's a discrepancy between these two statements?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me tell you. It is true maybe that is what I said, but this was ten years ago. But I am certain - and this will be confirmed by the others who were present there - that those same two soldiers, that they were there and that is what they said, and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Cvijanovic, you testified that ten of you soldiers headed towards the Vranjaca relay station.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you have in front of you, you told the Prosecution that there was some 15 of you HVO soldiers that headed towards Dusina and that 30 metres from the village you met Perica Rados and Mijo Ljubicic. And this is on page 3 of the B/C/S version, last paragraph. Are these two statements different too?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Things have been clarified, but let me clarify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. again. A squad of us ten started out, but more joined us, so that there were about 15 of us. And when we climbed up on the hill, the fire started -- was opened at us and Mijo Ljubicic came out from his house, where his father had been killed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the events yesterday and clarified it. I'm just trying to establish to what extent your statement given earlier and the statement here in court under oath are identical, to what extent they are identical. So will you please answer with a yes or no, if you can. Before I continue, since you mentioned that there were some differences in the translation, tell me, please: Did the Prosecution show you your statement before you started testifying here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one showed me anything. The statement I gave in 1999, at the time I signed it - and I stand by what I said. Now, how this was translated, it is impossible to have every word noted correctly, but the gist of it, the substance of it, is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that Zvonko Rajic had contacted Drago Rados because he had a radio station and that Rados told him that they had been attacked, that there were some killed and wounded, that there were people seeking aid, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Rajic called him and said that there were casualties, that there was a conflict going on, and he was asking for assistance. He told all of us this, and we heard him talk over the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement on page 2 you said: "Zvonko Rajic tried to contact the HVO commander Drago Rados who was at Brdo, but he could not get Drago on the radio." Again, these two statements differ.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Zvonko was establishing contact during the shooting in the morning, but Drago got -- reached Zvonko over the Motorola. There is a difference. Zvonko did call Drago and couldn't reach him, but Drago did reach Zvonko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated in court that when you opened fire as well, you managed to reach Perica Rados's house, that you were then joined by Perica Rados, Mijo Ljubicic, and Drago Rados. This is stated on page 71 of the transcript, lines 1 and 2. Did you say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, you stated that 30 metres before reaching the village you met Perica Rados and Mijo Ljubicic and you reached the house and managed to pull him out while the shooting was still going on. This is page 2, one-but-last sentence of the B/C/S document. Are these two statements different again?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what is written and what you are telling me, yes. But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my question. So the statements do differ. You also stated yesterday Zvonko Rados called up Busovaca again and that he was ordered to negotiate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Zvonko Rados. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Rajic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zvonko asked you to go with him but you didn't do that; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Zvonko called and then you're asking me about me going with him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that Zvonko spoke to Busovaca and received orders to negotiate. That is what you said.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, Zvonko Rajic asked you to go with him to those negotiations but you didn't accept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We started calling out to one another, and that is when the negotiations started. But Zvonko, upon Edin's initiative to go there, and no one dared go. And Edin was saying that he was guaranteeing that everything would be okay, and that is when Zvonko asked me to go with him but I simply didn't dare out of fear. I didn't trust them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to stop there because it is 10.30. We will have a 25-minute break, and we will resume at five to 11.00 with your cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]. You may be seated. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence again. And I should like to note that roughly speaking you will have about 30 minutes left for your cross-examination. The Prosecution yesterday took about an hour and a half, judging by my calculations. You've had an hour, which leaves you with 30 minutes. Of course, if the Prosecution wants to ask additional questions, it has the right to do so, and the Chamber might have one or two questions too. But anyway, I give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, I think we can continue. I think you've had a chance to have a rest. In your testimony yesterday, you said that Slavka Rados was the wife of Drago Rados and when she came to you she told you that civilians had been killed in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A similar statement was given by you to the OTP; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated before this court that you knew Edin Hakanovic from before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that he was a policeman in Visoko; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can also confirm that the town of Visoko does not belong to the Zenica municipality; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness. I'm afraid we cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how do you know that the town of Visoko belongs to the Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Cvijanovic. I sometimes ask questions that are clear to you and myself, but I'm asking you for the benefit of the other participants in this courtroom, to enable them to understand as well. Thank you. You know that there are proceedings against Mr. Hakanovic in Zenica at the moment, legal proceedings. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never said that you would testify in that case, although that is the duty of all citizens.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nobody ever asked me to do so. So how come you expect me to do that? How can I go to a court of law and do something like that? Now, had anybody asked me to testify, I would have agreed straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, yesterday you testified that at a point in time you saw a group of five or six soldiers who came in and that one of them had a flak jacket and the other one camouflage uniforms with black vests. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also asked by the Prosecutor - your response was that at that point, when you saw them, you didn't know who they actually were, and that was noted on page 81, line 3. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were going to Barucija to Radacove Kuce [phoen] near Crna, which is up on the hill from Crna towards the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said when asked by the Prosecutor that you didn't know Patkovic before the war but that you knew that during the war he negotiated with Zvonko Rajic and that on that day in the school he introduced himself personally. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said I didn't know him personally, but I did say that I heard what was going on, because I lived there, and I heard who the man was and what he was, but I didn't know him personally. And that Zvonko would tell us who he was and what he was because he negotiated with him. What they discussed, I don't know. But what I am telling you is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning, asked by the Prosecutor, you explained that at one point he went -- a gentleman entered the school you were in. He had a beard and a bag of Zvonko Rajic's, whom you saw for the first time then and there, and who ultimately introduced himself as being Serif Patkovic. Is that what you said this morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You interpreted that wrong, madam. It was the same man who was up at Brdo in the flak jacket, and I saw him very well and so did everybody else, not only me. And an unknown person entered and told us to stand before the man came in. I just described how -- what that man looked like, nothing more than that. So you misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave in 1999 to the investigators of the OTP, paragraph 2 in the B/C/S version, you stated the following: "I knew Patkovic by site before the war, and at the beginning of the war I would see him often at the checkpoints. He was then a deputy commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade." Do you agree that these statements differ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, once again you are interpreting things incorrectly. I didn't know him personally, and that's what I said. But I would see him around. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need to go on with your explanations. All I said was: Is that what you stated? And can you yourself see that the two statements differ?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know your interpretations or how you understand them. I can only say what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, last paragraph of that same statement, the 1999 statement, you state the following: "I saw a group of people coming from the direction of Dusina, and among them I recognised Serif Patkovic and Vahid, nicknamed Geler." However, that statement is quite contrary to what you said before that court.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, madam. I don't remember that. But what I said was I saw civilians walking across the field being led by armed soldiers. They had them in front of them. Now, I don't remember this other thing. Perhaps it was wrongly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you want to say is the investigator of The Hague Tribunal introduced into the statement something you did not actually say?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this. Perhaps the man understood it incorrectly; I don't know. Perhaps that's how they understood it. But what I told you I stand by. That's what I said. I saw what I saw and that's what I said, and it wasn't only I who was there myself. There were several other people, and I'm sure you'll hear it from them too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to the Court that from the place you were in you did not see how Rajic was wounded but you did hear just one shot and some noise, some commotion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you saw Rajic once again being carried by his brother and Franjo Batinic and Drago Rados; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the guys who were with them: Srecko Kristo, Jozo and Viktor Rajic, and his brother Perica Rados, Franjo Batinic, -- Srecko Kristo and Jozo Kristo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Cvijanovic, you also testified and said that Zvonko Rajic did not walk, that he was carried - that is on page 79, line 18 of the transcript - and then you said that Zvonko Rajic was lowered to the ground onto the mud and that the other soldiers were asked to place their hands up above their heads and look down at the ground. That was on page 79, lines 12 to 15. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, you said that Patkovic ordered the soldiers to place Zvonko Rajic in a line and that that's what they did, what the soldiers did, and that Zvonko Rajic tripped and fell into the stream. And that was noted on page 4, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Just a moment, please, but would you clarify that. I'm not quite clear on what you're saying or what you want. Would you go slowly, please, read it out slowly to me .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, in the middle of that paragraph, on page 4 of the B/C/S version, you said the following: "Then Patkovic ordered the soldiers to place Zvonko in a line and they shouted 'you Ustasha piece of shit.' The HVO soldiers put Zvonko in a line. Zvonko pleaded for help, and no response came. Zvonko tripped and fell into a ditch and Patkovic ordered the soldiers to put him out of the ditch, which they did."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that those two statements, as to the position of Zvonko Rajic, are completely different?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wasn't quoting each moment. I said roughly what was going on, the substance of it. I didn't explain all the details, because it lasted. It was an ongoing moment. It wasn't just one moment, one flash. And what I said basically - it depends how you want to look at it - but that's what I said, the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, as this was recorded in the transcript and in your own statement, this differs.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how this was translated and interpreted into English, and what they introduced into my statement, but what I said was that this was ten years ago and four years ago I gave that -- was when I gave that statement, so I can't remember every word of what I said. But basically I can explain something to you if something. If something is not clear to you, feel free to ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I will. You also said yesterday that after the murder, when Patkovic cocked his Skorpio pistol, after Zvonko Rajic's killing, he put his pistol to Drago Rajic to his forehead and pulled the trigger. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And several time by the Prosecutor in the course of the day yesterday you said that throughout the time you didn't budge from the place you were at when Zvonko Rajic went off with other HVO members and Edin Hakanovic. And that was noted on page 79, line 22; page 81, line 22/23; and in other places too. Now, is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that from that particular place you were able to see everything very well and that you were at a distance of about 50 to 70 metres as the crow flies from the place where the killing of Zvonko Rajic took place. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please. I said roughly what the distance was the way we saw it. It need not be exact. But yes, we were there, not only I myself but all the other people there too. And I gave the names as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
