utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, the one you gave to the Prosecutor, in the last paragraph, and page 4 in the first paragraph, you said: "I heard the Muslim soldiers ordering our group to let Zvonko go -- let him down, set him down. Then I moved down the hill with a couple of our soldiers, passing between the houses I saw a group which was coming from the direction of Dusina, and then I "I heard the Muslim soldiers ordering our group to let Zvonko go -- let him down, set him down. Then I moved down the hill with a couple of our soldiers. Passing between the houses I saw a group which was coming from the direction of Dusina, and then I was at a distance of 30 metres from the group. And from my position I was able to see everything and hear everything very well." Now, these two statements, Mr. Cvijanovic, are quite different; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, let me tell you this: I told you a moment ago I can't quote every word I said at the time. But I stand behind what I said that we were standing there. I don't know whether you know the house, whether you were ever there, whether you know what the area looks like. Now, the fact that we had to move around there and take shelter because there were hills all around --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, don't go into all these explanations. We've seen the general area and how the land lies. But you told the Prosecutor that you didn't move. I read out what you said in your statement, and the two things are not identical.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We moved around within a radius of 10, 20, 30 metres. They were shooting at us from all sides. It was a small field. But basically we stayed where we were. We didn't move from that general area and that position. If that's not clear to you, then I'll be happy to clarify it for you. Now, your interpretations are something else again. So moving around 10, 15, 20 metres, I consider that to be the same place, because they were shooting at us from all around. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you were not taken prisoner but that at Dragan Kristo's invitation, your neighbour, you went off to the same coffee bar you set off from that morning.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came from the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Kristo come to call you himself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement earlier on, you said that with Dragan Kristo Hazim Barucija came too. Once again, the two statements differ.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Faruk Barucija came to the billiard coffee bar. I said he -- that was wrongly interpreted. He came to the village of Visnjica; that's where he came. And when he arrived, he took from Ivica Kristo, nicknamed Peros [phoen], his wife and transferred him too and then he said that the Mujahedin had arrived and that along with lots of soldiers they said that unless we surrendered they would kill everyone. He told me that, and everybody will confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that same coffee bar, you encountered the two heavily armed members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they gave you information about their units to you as the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're interpreting this wrongly again. They didn't give us all the information, but they did talk to us. And the people were beside themselves. And they'll confirm that, I'm sure, because they couldn't believe that all that was going on. And I quote their words - and everyone will be able to tell you that, they will be able to tell you that too - they said, "I'm ashamed of being a Muslim." That's what they said. Those are their very words, and I'm quoting those words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you said that from the billiard coffee bar you set off towards the school building and that fire was opened on you, and that you returned again. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, the one you gave to the OTP, you said that you went straight from the coffee bar to the schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did go to the schoolhouse straight away. But when we were wondering whether to start off or not from the Gornja Visnjica area - and you can see everything down at the bottom quite clearly - they shot at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does thank you. I think we've clarified that point. But you also said that you were saved by a high-raping MUP officer. Bakir Alispahic was his name.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, because he conveyed that to me personally, after I was questioned in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the Minister of the Interior of the republican MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know the man. I heard him for the first time then. I heard him down there. He introduced himself. So I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I toll you that that high-ranking MUP officer of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not in Zenica at all at the time, would you agree with me there? I put it to you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the man. I knew how -- what he introduced himself, not only to me but to the others, because it was in the prison while we were in custody. And then we were led off to separate offices for interrogation, for questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You needn't go into all that. Now, asked by the Prosecutor today whether you were given medical assistance, you said that you were not given medical assistance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that as soon as we arrived, we weren't given assistance but later on that same man who questioned us and the gentleman who was the head there at the time, that a doctor did come in to the prison and gave us some medicines, et cetera. He gave us some assistance. And the assistance that we got was not anything that you could say helped us. It was just -- how shall I put this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijanovic. I didn't hear that part of your answer, and it wasn't recorded in the transcript, but you've clarified the point now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as almost every paragraph stated by this -- uttered by this witness to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal is contrary to what he has said in court, I suggest that the statement given to the OTP be tendered into evidence and it goes to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to your demand to have this tendered into evidence, the Prosecution wishes to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the comments by my learned colleague perhaps would have been better saved for argumentation. Be that as it may, if she could simply clarify for the record whether she's tendering this statement purely as it might go to the credibility of the witness or whether she's tendering it for the truth of the matter set forth in the document would be a helpful clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could the Defence define more precisely the object it has in mind in tendering this. Is it to contest the credibility of the witness, to test the credibility of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender the statement into evidence in order to assert the lack of credibility of this witness and not to assert the facts as presented in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, previously you made a statement with respect to the events that you testified about today. And I should like to ask you to be shown the statement you gave to the Commission for the Establishment of War Crimes, Mostar, taken by Jure Kristo, the representative of that commission. I think I have handed round sufficient copies for Their Honours and the rest of the participants. I'm sorry, this statement exists only in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, lets assign a number to the statement taken by the OTP of this witness. May we have a number, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is DH4 and DH4 B/C/S for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, we have a second document. Has this document been translated into English?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we have already informed you, with respect to translation problems, this document has not been translated into English. I hope that the Trial Chamber will make suggestions as to what to do in future with respect to translation issues, because all the documents for cross-examination for Dusina have been returned to us by the registrar in their original. I should like to have a number assigned to this document, because it will be tendered into evidence later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give -- to mark it for identification. May we do that now, please. I see the Prosecutor on his feet with respect to this B/C/S document, that it hasn't been translated yet. May we hear your comments. The Defence wishes to produce it. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position would be the same with respect to the document marked DH2 for identification; namely, we have not seen this document. It's not in one of the official working languages. And we respectfully reserve our position on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to assign a provisional number to the document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is DH5 ID, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn to the Defence now to tell us of the weight the document holds -- the gist of the document, the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should first of all like to ask Mr. Cvijanovic to tell us whether he recognises his signature on pages 1 and 2, and then I'll go on to explain the contents of the document to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, did you in fact sign this document on pages 1 and 2? Take a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me read through it, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you to take a look at the signature first and then we'll discuss the contents later.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is identical to my signature, but whether it is mine I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I proceed with my questions to the witness pertaining to this document? Because he said that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the Prosecution would object. There's not a proper foundation. The witness has said he doesn't remember the document. He said the signature is identical to his but whether it is his he cannot say; "I do not know." The Prosecution would assert there's no proper foundation for asking the witness questions about this document, given his previous response to the last two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At this point the Chamber notes that the witness has some doubts as to the signature. He can raise those doubts but tell us whether he knows what the document is about. And I'm going to give him several minutes to look through the document. And we can have the document placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I give clarification and tell you what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed, let's hear from the witness. Is this a real document or a false document? Because he seems to have doubts about his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but first of all, can I ask who this man Jure Kristo is to whom the lady refers and to -- the document she is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a document from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Mr. Kristo?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna is what it says, the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Commission for Establishing War Crimes on the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar took a statement from Zeljko Cvijanovic, son of Zarko, with his personal data, and a representative of the commission taking the statement was this man Jure Kristo. That is what it states after all the particulars of the witness, Zeljko Cvijanovic, is set out in the first paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just know one man named Jure Kristo. I don't remember this, however. This is an unimportant document, as far as I'm concerned. Jure Kristo was a gentleman who was my neighbour. He lived in Germany. He lived and worked -- has been living and working in Germany for many years. It is his house, however, in which the billiard coffee bar is located, and one of his relatives was a proprietor, and that's the Kristo I know. I don't remember this particular Kristo, and this is incorrect, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, did you at any time make a statement to the Commission for the Establishment of War Crimes at all, before you made the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO CVIJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to ask me, madam. What commission are you referring to? What kind of commission? I absolutely have no recollection of any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is going to ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Jure Kristo, who questioned you about events that you witnessed, and did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't remember. Very well. Please proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, in this statement, in paragraph 3, you said the following: "I was at Dusina --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has clearly said he has no recollection of appearing before any such commission or giving any such statement. The Prosecution would assert it's improper for the Defence to cross-examine him quoting from a document which he clearly does not recall or have any knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This document is contested formally by the witness; therefore, in that case you cannot continue to question him about it, because this could be considered pressure on the witness who is contesting the authenticity of this document. Therefore, this document cannot be admitted. Do you have any other questions to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my understanding is that this document has been identified nevertheless and that it will be possible in the course of these proceedings to establish the authenticity of the document. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, you understood perfectly, that there will be time for the Defence to produce it with other evidence. Do you have any other questions for this witness? Because it's already 11.35.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just two more questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijanovic, you will agree with me when I say that the conflict in Dusina started the moment when members of the HVO killed Camdzic, who was going to negotiate with you.

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I never saw that man in my life, nor did I ever negotiate, so that was absolutely not so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will also agree with me that you shot at this man from a sniper and that that was the reason why you didn't surrender immediately and why you hid.

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I think those are pure fabrications, and personally, after everything, my conclusion on the basis of everything that happened in Lasva is that prior to the attack on Busovaca, when the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina thought it would enter easily, what you said is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the cross-examination, the Defence tells us that it has no further questions, so I give the floor now to the Prosecution, which, pursuant to Article 85 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, may now re-examine the witness, following the questions put by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interject on behalf of Mr. Kubura. Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. On behalf of Mr. Kubura --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Realtime transcript read in error "There are questions"] -- questions to be asked of this witness on behalf of Mr. Kubura. As Your Honours will know, he hasn't been charged with events in Dusina or for any events before 1 April, 1993, which are the matters that this witness has dealt with, and indeed in the list of witnesses which is provided by the Prosecution with the pre-trial brief for Your Honours, he is not marked as a witness who is relevant for Mr. Kubura. There are a number of witnesses on that list that are not marked as relevant for him, and in most of those cases the Defence for Mr. Kubura will not be asking questions of those witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Dixon. The Prosecutor, do you wish to ask any additional questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But just for -- for a matter of clarification, it would appear in the English transcript that Mr. Dixon indicated that there are questions to be asked of this witness on behalf of Mr. Kubura, and simply to clarify that. I'm not sure if -- if that's a misquote in the transcript or if in fact the Defence for Mr. Kubura does have questions for this witness. So perhaps if that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any questions for this witness. It's a misquote in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for the witness. And I might ask that he be shown Defence Exhibit DH4, the statement that he provided to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal. Does he have both the English and the B/C/S? If they could both be placed before the witness, please. Re-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you DH4, the statement that you gave to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. You have both the English and the B/C/S version of that statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign one of those versions of that statement?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: Yes. It's DH4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign the English version or the B/C/S version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I signed in my own language. The signature is here, which corresponds to my signature. And when I made my statement, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me -- let me --

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the versions of the document - the statement that you have before you - is in the English language, and one version of that statement is in the Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian or Serbo-Croatian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you signed, was it the English version or was it the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I signed indicating my identity number. When I made the statement there was a lady. I think it was written in our language and that it was translated into English. I can't remember exactly, but I know that I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Can you please look through the document that you have signed, the text of the document that you have signed. Is that document in English or in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: In English. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you read or speak the English language?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: No, I don't speak the English language, nor am I able to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the B/C/S version of your statement, which is before you, the version in a language that you can read. Did you in fact sign the B/C/S version of your statement that you provided to the Tribunal investigator?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time you ever saw the Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian language version of the statement that you provided the investigator?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: That was in Vitez, when I made my statement. Then the gentleman showed it to me, and I signed it when I was making the statement there. This was, I think, in the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you sign a B/C/S version of your statement, or did you only sign the English version?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: The lady read out to me, and I signed it in English, I think, the English version. I remember that well. It was in the elementary school in Vitez. But I can't tell you exactly. I do know that I signed the statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has a question for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to know whether the witness speaks Arabic or understands Arabic.

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: I don't speak Arabic, but before the war I worked for a time in Arab countries, so that I was working there and I was able to identify the people speaking that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that when you heard Muslims speaking Arabic, you were able sometimes to understand what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: No, I couldn't understand what those words meant, but I heard what they were saying. I don't speak Arabic. I don't understand the words and what they mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard but you didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: Do you remember appearing before a commission represented by
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have any questions? No questions. In that case, your testimony is now over. Thank you for coming to The Hague to testify as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey home. You are free to leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have a witness as envisaged. Regarding the timing, we can begin with his examination up until 12.30, when we will have our usual break, and we will resume at five to 1.00, until 1.45. So the usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you hearing what I'm saying in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us your first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Franjo Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th of September, 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am living in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now or before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, currently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am attached to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are a career military man.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: And what is your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldier first class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, soldier first class. Very well. I hear that you have -- I see that you had a headphone -- a cap in your hand. You can't wear it, but you are first going to read the solemn declaration given to you. Will you please read the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. The Prosecution will now ask you questions. So I give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution. We have until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we anticipate this examination of Franjo Batinic, the second Prosecution witness, lasting for about 1 hour 15 or 1 hour 30 minutes. The examination-in-chief will focus on the murder of Zvonko Rajic and on the mistreatment of the witness in the Zenica Music School in the order as just mentioned. Examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you been in the Yugoslav army, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber when and where.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: In 1987, I went to Karlovac, close to Zagreb, where I served working on pontoon bridges. And I completed my service on the 10th of June, 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there any time you joined another military organisation?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "military organisation"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the JNA -- what did you do after you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Military organisation -- nothing -- I'm sorry. I found a job in the Primorje-Rijeka company in Zenica. I worked there for about three months. And then I worked temporarily for three months and 29 days. After that, my brother from Switzerland came with a tractor and I worked with a tractor. I tilled the land. I worked on the farm up until the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the conflict. Did you ever join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question: Did you ever join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the acronym HVO stand for?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: HVO. It's units of the Croatian Defence Council, of the Croatian people, HVO for short, for defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where? What unit were you attached to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: A reconnaissance platoon, Lasva, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, towards the end of 1992, when you already have been a member of the HVO, were there any tensions in the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. The conflict started in Busovaca afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What conflict, Witness, are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the conflict in Lasva. And I am testifying about the late Zvonko Rajic, the conflict when they attacked -- the 7th Muslim attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who were the opposing sides of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: We were attacked. The Muslim party attacked us, and the Serbs had left the area before that. They had moved out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification, are you saying that the parties of the conflict were the HVO and the ABiH, the armed forces of the government of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before 1992, before the end of 1992, how was the relation between the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: In 1992, the HVO did not exist, but the relationship between the population was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any changes towards the end of 1992 and/or at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify a little, please, your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were saying that in the course of 1992 the different ethnicities within the area of Busovaca and Central Bosnia were living quite well together. You were saying that there were changes afterwards. What signs of changes can you describe for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: It's a rather difficult question for me, I'm afraid. Maybe if I put my cap on I would be able to answer. About the conflicts in Lasva, you find that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have been told by the President that you are not allowed to wear your cap here and there's no need for it, obviously.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Never mind, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, to move on -- in January 1993, were there any Muslim soldiers in the area of Lasva?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: There were. They were stationed down there at the Usce, at the confluence, at the crossroads, for about 15 days, maybe a little longer. That's where they were staying. My brother has a house there. It used to be state-owned, and there were machine-gun nests around there and they were on duty there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And such Muslim soldiers you are referring to, were they members of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The army of BiH, they were all under the army of the BiH. There were several units under them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, for the interpreters could you help the witness with the microphone, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask without the presence of the witness for me to inform the Trial Chamber of a fact that may be of relevance for the testimony of this witness. I am not quite sure whether the Prosecutor is aware of this fact. I didn't know whether this fact was true, but in view of the first answers given by the witness, perhaps it would be opportune for members of the Trial Chamber to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer the witness to leave the courtroom for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, in the absence of the witness, because your question -- your information could raise a problem with respect to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution doesn't know what Defence counsel are referring to; however, we would agree to such a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, Mr. Usher, will you please take the witness outside the courtroom for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him be close by in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this part of the hearing be in private session, please? Could the public be excluded? Because it could have consequences for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us order private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecutor for him to proceed with his questions. But before you go ahead, let me tell the witness that he can answer the questions asked of him but if he feels that he is unable to answer, he should not do so and that if he doesn't understand a question sufficiently clearly, he can ask that the question be repeated until he understands it fully. Does the witness understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you still recall where you have been on the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, I left my house and went to Brdo. That's where I spent the night. We toured the stables with some colleagues, the barn, and that's where I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far away Brdo is from Dusina, the hamlet of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, Brdo from Dusina? I said about 2 or 3 kilometres, perhaps less. You have to go across the fields, and then it's quicker. It's quite near. It's a hamlet, underneath Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night from the 25th to the 26th of January 1993, you spent in a stable near Brdo. Can you inform the Trial Chamber how you did awake the next day.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in the stable or barn. We just checked on it, because my father had his livestock there, his sheep, so we checked on that and went to Perica Rados's house and that's where I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perica Rados's house, where is it located?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Perica Rados's house is at Brdo. It's a hamlet of Dusina. It belongs to the late Niko Rados, actually, the house, but he's not the eldest one there. He was in Zenica and abroad, his brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, on 26 January 1993, how did you awake?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, I awoke -- my colleagues went outside and I heard some shooting, so I jumped up and went outside. And we were attacked from the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard some shootings and you were attacked from the surrounding area. Where did the shootings come from and who did attack you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Who shot? Well, the 7th Muslim, the one that attacked us. They shot from up there, the Barucija house. It's a house with a big roof, square roof. It was green in colour. They looked for shelter, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When 7th Muslim Brigade shot at you, how many soldiers were around at the area at this time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: At that time? Well, I couldn't count them at that time. I just realised when we met up, then I saw how many of them in that area, but around Dusina there that's where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have any recollection being about 3 kilometres away from Dusina what happened in Dusina at the same time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you could hear shooting up there. But as I say, I can't talk about Dusina when I wasn't up there myself. All I can tell you was about Brdo and the sounds that were heard round about, and about Zvonko Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shooting you heard, at what time in the morning was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: 5.30, half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the shooting you heard in Brdo and the shooting you heard in Dusina, was it at about at the same time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, a bit earlier. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to sit closer to the microphones. Thank you. We're having trouble hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please clarify whether the shooting in Brdo and the shooting in Dusina was at the same time.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, round about. At Dusina it was a little earlier, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to Brdo, who was your commander in Brdo at the time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Dragan Rados. Well, all right, he was some sort of deputy of Zvonko's, I think. And there was German too. Ivo Filipovic, he was asked about things too. No, German stayed on down there. Rados was up there at Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And beside him, who was the local commander, the local HVO commander for the Lasva area?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: That was Rajic Zvonko. Zvonko Rajic, he was the main commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic, has he been --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- present when the attack at Brdo started?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: No. Zvonko was down there, Donja Visnjica, Rajici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any time that day when Zvonko Rajic joined you in Brdo or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course he did, after some time had gone by. Some soldiers stayed down there; others went up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zvonko Rajic join you in Brdo?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did join us. And he died up there. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber at about what time -- at about how many hours after the commencement of the fighting Zvonko Rajic joined you in Brdo.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour, an hour and a half to two hours. An hour and a half, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time Zvonko Rajic joined you, was the fighting still ongoing and continuing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Well, all right, it had calmed down. There was a lull. But up until half past 9.00, then we surrendered and ... came to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You entered into an agreement. Can you please provide the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please provide the Trial Chamber further details on that agreement.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The agreement with ...? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The agreement you were just referring to. And you were referring to an agreement in respect to your surrender.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, about 9.30, from Dusina, Dragan Rados's wife came, I think with Hakanovic, Edin. And Edin stayed down there in the field. Dragan's wife came up to us to convey to us. She came with the civilians. The civilians also came down there, and she came to tell us to surrender and to agree on something. And then they agreed somehow that unless we surrender, unless we surrender our rifles and come to an arrangement the civilians would be killed. And when she got there, Zvonko went down the hill for negotiations and allegedly they put their rifles on their backs and we went to the Ivo Lola Ribar primary school and we all got together there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person who decided on the surrender -- on your surrender?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic. Well, actually, it wasn't surrender. No, we went down there to negotiate and reach an agreement and do what was to be done. Zvonko negotiated. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to certain conditions. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what the conditions were about.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that. I wasn't listening carefully enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring, Mr. Batinic, to conditions for the surrender. Can you please explain for the Trial Chamber what such conditions were about.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: To surrender, to stop the shooting. However, had I known that that would have happened, they wouldn't have surrendered -- I wouldn't have surrendered. Because when we surrendered, I went down towards the school all together, and there was a Muslim soldier there who was killed and -- yes, he was a soldier. And the four of us picked him up and carried him towards Crna Zemlja and then a cart and horse turned up and they were able to take him away. And when -- but before that, one of the soldiers, Mijo Ljubicic, we sent down there, because there was one other soldier of ours left down there in Donja Visnjica to lay down his weapon and to go to the schoolhouse to negotiate, for the television to come in to film it all. But this soldier --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, may I please interrupt you at this point. After your surrender, did you still carry -- did the HVO soldiers still carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: We did up to Vodica. And then from Dusina, Omer Vehida, somebody informed him, someone from the army and the unit, told him that there would be an ambush at Donja Visnjica, where our soldiers were located. And of course, they cocked their rifles at us. They took off -- well, the bombs they had or whatever, the rifles that we -- the rifles that we had on our shoulders and the other ammunition we were carrying, they took it all off us, and sent us back where the fighting was and we had to go across that area, Crna Zemlja and Usce, not to pass through Donja Visnjica but to take the other route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you escorted by HVO 7th Muslim Brigade soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, one group stayed down there, and the other group went towards Tuzla, and the ones that escorted us mistreated the late Zvonko and he said -- they said, "Where are your heavy weapons and your mines and hand grenades?" And had we had any heavy weapons, we wouldn't have surrendered in the first place. And of course we started off up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did the soldiers did mistreat Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, they mistreated him -- how shall I say? They wanted him to own up and tell them where he had buried and hidden the weapons, because we didn't -- he thought they -- we didn't only have light weapons and mortars, small calibre, 60 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mistreatment you are referring to, can you provide the Trial Chamber more detail on this mistreatment and what happened to Zvonko Rajic that day.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: That day, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe how he was killed and who did kill him.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, he was killed by Serif Patkovic. And let me explain how this happened. We went up from Vodica towards Brdo. We were returning on the battle ground up there. And we reached the point where you turn towards Vranjaca to the new road, and that's where the late Zvonko succumbed. He couldn't take it psychologically any more; we couldn't either. But what could you do? You were in their hands. And he was trying to escape that way. And several metres on he started running, trying to flee. They took up their rifles. There was a burst of gunfire, two or three of them, and of course they hit him. He was shot in the leg and up here in his shoulder. It was an entrance/exit wound. And he fell down. When they reached him, they started kicking him with their feet. He screamed, of course, when they reached him, they started kicking him with their feet. He screamed, of course, and they said, "Come on, you four. Carry him off." And we started carrying him up the hill towards Brdo. And then further on, further up, and we carried him -- oh, I don't know how many metres. You know the lie of the land there -- up to Brdo. And Zvonko said, "I've been wounded. Can you get some first aid?" And Patkovic took his Skorpio pistol and fire all the ammunition -- all the bullets that were in the pistol, fired at his head. And he was dead. We are still carrying him. He was in our hands, arms. We set him down on the ground then and he cocked his rifle at us and he said, "Is there anybody else who's wounded?" So we put him down. They shoved him over, kicked him over towards a tree. And that's where we stood. And then they shot another few bursts of gunfire at him. And that would be that, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For verification, you were amongst the four people -- or were you amongst the four people who carried Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was. I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away have you been when Serif Patkovic killed Zvonko Rajic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I was right next to him. I was holding him. Whether it was by his legs or somewhere else -- but anyway, I was right next to his body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serif Patkovic, how did you know that it was Serif Patkovic who killed him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that man, but there are some commanders who knew him. Zvonko Rajic knew him. There was some of our men who knew him. I saw him on television maybe, but otherwise I didn't know him. I never saw him again close up. I may have come across him in Zenica, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's about 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to adjourn for 25 minutes, and we will resume work at five to 1.00. So could the witness please wait and not speak to anyone during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] . Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, before the break, we talked about the murder of Zvonko Rajic. After he has been killed, what happened to you and the other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: When Zvonko was killed, I told you they pushed him down to the pear tree. Then they tied us up. Some people had their hands behind their backs, others around their heads. And they took us to Usce from this hill. Do I need to explain how that happened? On the way down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm more interested in the treatment or mistreatment. What did the ABiH soldiers do to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: There on the spot, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the spot, on the way down.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The BH army or the 7th Muslim, but they were all under the same command. It was the 7th Muslim that was there. There was mistreatment. First the man who killed Zvonko asked whether there were any relatives among the four of us that were carrying him, and his brother, Viktor Rajic, was there but he didn't dare say that he was there because if he had, he would have killed him. So people kept quiet. There was some mistreatment and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This mistreatment, what was it about?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Curses, you know. "We'll kill you too," and things like that. Somebody would be hit here and there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you yourself been the object of such mistreatment, such hits?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just then I kept quiet, so they didn't hit me there. No, he just pointed his gun at us, asking whether there was anyone else who was wounded. But as for beatings, I wasn't beaten then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, where have you been taken to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the music school in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who took you to the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Soldiers who happened to be there. There was a local too. There was a bus waiting for us at the confluence of the two rivers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These locals who you are referring to, were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This man who escorted us, Batan, he was wearing civilian clothes. But I didn't see whether he had a rifle. He probably did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you forced to be brought to the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: They tied us up. That was by force. They -- when they tied us up mind our backs, and some people behind the neck, of course it was by force. If he has a rifle if his hand, you have to do as he says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you arrived in the Zenica Music School, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Then the interrogations started. They took us into a hall, a rather large room. There was a stage there. There were chairs put there. We sat down and one by one went upstairs. I suppose he was deputy commander, who interrogated us, asking what happened. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: When it was my turn -- first of all, when we were sitting on the stage, a man walked in and slapped each and every one of us. One of them did offer some cigarettes. And when it was my turn to go upstairs for interrogation, I went into a room and then they asked us, "Where are your weapons, your mortars? Where have you dug them? Are they in the caves? Where are they?" Then I said 10 German marks -- I had 10 German marks on me and I handed them over. They were saying that they would kill us if we didn't tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were hit. Was there any other form of mistreatment of you or any of the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I can talk of myself in that room. But people went in one by one. We didn't go in there all together. First it was in order. I can't remember which one I was in order. There was mistreatment there -- not there. They beat in another room. The beating was in another room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you been the victim of such a beating?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I wish I hadn't been. In this other room that they took us to, then they beat shoulders and chests most. Do you want to have water in your knee? We spent some time there. Later on they transferred us to where we would be staying, and we stayed there for three or four days -- four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to the Zenica Music School, the beatings, can you provide more details to the Trial Chamber. What were the means -- by what means were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I can explain. Pieces of wood about this size, about 80 centimetres long, in the form of the bats they use in that game, and they hit us with it on the back, and they also kicked us. My chest was all black and blue and my shoulders, my eyebrow had been slit when one of them kicked me. That was also black and blue. Of course, sometimes they would hit me with a rifle too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether other detainees have also been beaten?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, they did. Kristo was there, this other colleague of mine. He was there. They were beaten even worse. He would give in immediately. He'd start crying. I couldn't cry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody else who has been beaten you can recall?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There were five of us there -- five or six -- six of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they all beaten?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were beaten. I was the youngest among them. I was 26 years old and 4 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they have been beaten using the same means to beat them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't talk about someone else. That other person will tell you what he was beaten with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described your wounds. Have you seen similar wounds inflicted on other people?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. In the music school I was beaten only that one, that evening. They didn't beat me down there. Others were beaten. The locals would tell certain people what they had done, and they -- and they should be beaten. But one colleague of mine saved me. He came with friends. Maybe he also came to beat. But when he saw me, he said, "Leave him alone." And after that, no one beat me again in the music school. Only that evening, when I was up there in the room for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was actually beating you? Who were the people beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The prisoners, they were all from the outside. There was one, a colleague of Viktor Rajic's, who used to work with him, and this one who recognised me, he could also testify who did the beating, but I didn't know those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From outside, you are referring to the detainees; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, the soldiers who were beating us. They were not locals. I didn't know them. According to stories, apparently they had come from Krajina, maybe from another municipality. I don't know. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who operated the Zenica Music School as a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but where they interrogated us there was someone with a little beard. Now, whether his name was Jasmin, I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have military uniforms. They took off boots or jackets from our soldiers; then they were dressed properly. Some people had civilian clothes; somebody -- some wore jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you remember that you have been interviewed by investigators -- by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. I remember. In 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I had started building my house. I still haven't finished it. Yes. I can't give you the date. It was in November -- no, no, maybe October, something like that, when we had this conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you on the screen in both in English and B/C/S your statement you've given. Can you identify your signature on this statement, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I can. I can sign it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know why the Prosecutor is showing this statement to the witness. The Prosecutor should lay the foundations first if he is going to proclaim the witness is a hostile witness. I see no reason why a witness who testified for this Tribunal should be shown his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I assume that the Prosecutor is going to respond to your question, but he certainly wants to tender this statement. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to do so. And I wish to use the 1999 statement for the purpose to allow the witness to clarify who operated the 7th -- the Zenica Music School.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we object. The Prosecutor has no legal basis to show the statement to the witness or to tender it to the Trial Chamber, except to disqualify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We wish to refresh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We wish to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we will now show you page 6 of the statement. In the second paragraph from the top, the second sentence reads as follows - and you please compare in the B/C/S -- would you please have a look at the B/C/S version - There is written "The two officers contained 7th Muslim Brigade flags." Can you read this? It's now highlighted on your screen.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Read the portion which you find on your screen right now.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: "With the completion of the questioning, I was taken to another office where the same procedure commenced. The two officers contained 7th Muslim Brigade flags. After the beating, I was taken away and offered some food. It was about 11.00 p.m. when the beatings stopped."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall having said this to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object once again, Your Honours. Pursuant to Rule 92 bis, it is clearly stated when and for what reasons a statement may be used may be used and a statement cannot be used to prove anything other -- it cannot be used to prove the responsibility. As this affects the responsibility of my client, the Prosecutor is showing this statement contrary to the Rules and I appeal to the Chamber to sustain our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem raised by the Defence is the following: The witness heard by the Office of the Prosecutor testified that during the interrogation he saw two flags. Therefore, the Prosecution wants the witness to confirm what he said in his written statement, as he signed that document at the time. The Defence is challenging this approach, and in fact it is a minor point. The Prosecution could easily have asked the witness whether during the interrogation he saw these two flags. The witness would have said, "Yes, I remember it," and then the Prosecution could have shown him this document. Actually, the objection of the Defence is quite negligible. It is simply a matter of procedure which boils down to the same because in any event what the Prosecution is trying to show is that the witness saw certain material elements during his interrogation. Is that indeed the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution, Mr. President, will not tender the statement into evidence. What I'm currently doing is to refresh the memory of the witness. The statement has been taken in 1999; at that point in time, four years ago, the witness may have had a better recollection as he does have today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, you are not asking to tender this statement into evidence. Maybe the Defence will ask for that. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, I think that this is a question which is of quite considerable importance today. We are at the beginning of this trial, and I think it is important to have a good understanding of the way in which we are going to question all the witnesses in this Chamber. When a witness is called to testify viva voce, it is because there's a reason to call him because he's going to tell the Chamber the things he remembers and not what he learnt from his statement -- or taken from his statement. Before the witness appears here, the Prosecution meets with the witness and can even talk to him and remind him of things before he appears in the chamber, a procedure that is quite exceptional in many systems. Here we have a witness appearing before you, and they wish to remind him on the basis of a statement, to refresh his memory. The only permissible procedure of refreshing the memory of a witness is to refer to personal notes, if he has any notes that belong to him, a document that belongs to him. In that case, the permission of the Chamber may be requested to -- for the witness to refresh his memory on the basis of notes that he took himself. And then those notes may be admitted into evidence. In the case of a statement given by the witness to the Office of the Prosecutor, the only -- when such a statement may be used, in our submission, is if the Prosecution wants to declare the witness hostile. If the witness's answers are in contrast to what he said in the statement, then the Prosecutor can say to the Chamber that he wishes this witness to be declared hostile because he's saying things that are in contradiction to what he said then. So he may declare the witness hostile. This is quite different from what is happening in the cross-examination, because the purpose of the cross-examination or one of those aims is to contradict the witness with the help of his statement. But here we are dealing with the examination-in-chief, and we are -- we submit, with all due respect, that the Prosecution may not use a statement of the witness to refresh his memory. An example that you gave, Mr. President, with all due respect, you said that the Prosecutor could have asked him, "Did you see flags in the room?" However, we could immediately object because we could say that that is a tendentious or leading question. To suggest to the witness that he saw flags is a question that cannot normally be put in an examination-in-chief. For all these reasons, Mr. President, we request that you make a ruling regarding the use of witness statements, and this is a matter of principle that goes quite beyond this rather minor matter of fact. But as we are at the beginning of the trial, I think it is important to have a ruling so as -- so that we might know why the use of a statement may be allowed to refresh the witness's memory. It doesn't matter whether we are talking about the Anglo-Saxon system or the German or Romanic system, but we do submit, with due respect, that such statements cannot be used to refresh the memory of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So the Defence is telling us that in its view the Prosecution should address questions to the witness without using any documents and that the witness should spontaneously testify in response to questions on facts of which he was a direct witness, on the basis of questions put to him, and at the same time produce -- to produce a written document in which the witness has already given his position would risk, in the position of the Defence, to -- risking -- to induce the witness to respond in a manner in which this would be prejudicial to the accused. Therefore, the Defence wishes the examination to take place orally and then, within the framework of the cross-examination, the Defence may put questions relying possibly on documents, as it did so with the previous witness, and that then the Prosecution may on the basis of Rule 85 re-examine the witness. So regarding these submissions of the Defence. Before the Chamber rules, what is the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence is raising a number of issues that are missing the point. This is not an issue related to Rule 92 bis. We are not tendering the prior statement, the statement into evidence. It is not a hostile, obviously -- it's obviously not a hostile witness. There are no contradictions. The witness was not in a position to detail, to describe for the Trial Chamber which military units have operated the Zenica Music School. In his statement given four years ago -- given more than four years ago to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, he obviously had a better recollection, and I am -- I am about to ask him whether this recollection in 1999 reflects his memory of the facts in 1999. And that's all what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it is 1.30 -- and how much more time do you need for your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I anticipate that I can finish within the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes? In that case, the cross-examination can start tomorrow, and then the witness has to come back. More so, as I understand there's a problem with tomorrow's witness, who is stuck at Sarajevo airport because of the fog. So in any event, this witness will come back tomorrow. And in the meantime, the Chamber will be able to respond to the question raised. Continue your examination, but without using the written statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prisoners, the detainees in the Zenica Music School, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: You mean the ones that were brought there or whether there were any more civilians? As far as the soldiers are concerned, six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many civilians? You were referring to civilians.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: The civilians, when the conflict started in Lasva, or the Dusina hill, down there the Croats were stopped. They stopped a man I knew from Drvuse. He started out in his Mercedes, an old type of Mercedes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Witness, how many civilians were imprisoned in the Zenica Music School --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Two or three, thereabout. Three or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about their --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: While we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Oh, they were Croats, yes, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were all Croats or were there also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Leading question. I object to the leading form the question took.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In my understanding, it's not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there detainees from other ethnicities than Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Because Drvuse is further away, further from Lasva. I knew this one man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one man, was he of a different ethnicity than the Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: What? Croat, he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were mentioning some minutes ago that at some point in time you have been transferred. For how long have you been imprisoned in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Three and a half to four days. We weren't there for one whole day. Then they transferred us. They brought in a kombi van to the KP Dom, a Renault 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The KP Dom, where is it located, the KP Dom you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you go to Crna, and then further up, to the exit on Zenica on the right-hand side, taking the old road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For clarification, are you referring to the Zenica KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Zenica KP Dom, where we were transferred to by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That completes the examination-in-chief. I suggest that the Defence should take the floor tomorrow and start the cross-examination, because we've just got a few minutes left of this session. But as we do have, in fact, ten minutes left, I'm going to ask the Defence would they like to go ahead and start their cross-examination today or wait for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to follow your proposal and begin tomorrow and have our cross-examination take place in one lump.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what about the Kubura Defence? May we have their views.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour. We will, if there are to be any questions, do those tomorrow, after the team for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, that the Chamber is aware that we have, due to weather conditions in Sarajevo, a bit of a problem to bring the witness tomorrow for the early hours. The witness will, at the earliest, arrive at 10.00 -- will be in the country at the earliest at 10.00. So we suggest to commence with the next witness not earlier than by noon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So -- the third witness? Is that what you mean? You're going to bring in your third witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm referring to the third witness. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At all events, we begin tomorrow morning at 9.00 with the cross-examination by the Defence, and it will last approximately an hour and a half. With the breaks, that will make it time for you to bring your third witness in. So before we take up our session -- when we take up our session tomorrow, the Chamber will have a ruling with respect to the queries made by the Defence regarding the documents and the statement taken by the OTP simultaneously with the oral testimony. So we'll make our ruling tomorrow and give it to you before we start tomorrow morning. Witness, you will come back here tomorrow morning at 9.00 for the continuation of your testimony, and you will be answering questions put to you by the Defence teams of the two accused. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question, please? May I be allowed to ask something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the flight is concerned, will that be all right? Because my flight -- my return flight to Sarajevo is scheduled for tomorrow. Will that be all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What time is your flight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 10.30, something like that, from Amsterdam airport. If it's all right, no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not up to the Trial Chamber, of course, to see to material issues of that nature regarding your return flight, but you should ask the relevant services. If we begin the cross-examination tomorrow morning at 9.00, you'll still be here at 10.30, so you won't be able to make your flight at 10.30. So it is up to the registrar -- Registry to sort the matter out. And of course, Madam Registrar, will see to that question. But we will see you back here tomorrow morning at 9.00. Having said that, I adjourn the meeting until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: 1.35 p.m. to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of December, 2003 at 9.00 a.m.
